questions.title: What does "substantial evidence" review actually let a court of appeals do in an asylum case?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture here. The Tenth Circuit keeps saying it reviews the BIA's factual findings for "substantial evidence" and cannot reweigh the record unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to reach the opposite result. In practice, how deferential is that? If the record could support either side, does the noncitizen basically lose on petition for review? I'm trying to understand why the court spends so much time saying there was "substantial evidence" for the BIA instead of deciding for itself whether these facts amount to persecution or political targeting.

questions.title: Why weren't repeated death threats, being held at gunpoint, and the incident involving the child enough to count as past persecution?
questions.question_body: The opinion says courts look at incidents cumulatively, not one by one. Here the family got repeated threatening phone calls, a brochure saying "death to snitches from Liberal Party," Jimenez was held at gunpoint, armed men later came back and assaulted an employee while looking for the family, and then a stranger put a hand over the son's mouth and told him to run to his dad. Even if there was no lasting physical injury, this seems much more serious than just verbal harassment. What is the doctrinal line between "serious threats" and persecution in asylum law, especially when the threats are repeated and accompanied by armed confrontations?

questions.title: How did the court decide political opinion was only tangential when the threats mentioned the Liberal Party and said they were "in politics"?
questions.question_body: The nexus part is where I get most lost. The court says the main motive was Jimenez's involvement with Don Rafa's property and criminal operation, not the family's political opinion. But some of the threats explicitly referenced the Liberal Party, and the attackers also called them "snitches for the police" who were "in politics." In a mixed-motive case, how do courts figure out whether political opinion is "one central reason" instead of just incidental? Does the timing of the escalation after the property dispute outweigh the explicit political language in the threats?

questions.title: Does an asylum applicant usually need to file a formal police report to prove the government was unable or unwilling to protect them?
questions.question_body: The court seemed to put a lot of weight on the fact that Petitioners only spoke to two individual police officers and did not really pursue the matter further, despite claiming police corruption and government ties to Don Rafa. I understand that lack of reporting can undercut the claim, but how formal does the reporting have to be? Is talking to patrol officers ever enough to put the government on notice? And what kind of evidence is usually needed to show that reporting would have been futile or dangerous, so the failure to report does not sink the claim?

questions.title: Who bears the burden on internal relocation when past persecution was not established, and why did three weeks with relatives matter so much?
questions.question_body: The relocation discussion confused me because the court says Petitioners already failed to show eligibility for asylum, but then it still says they could safely relocate within Colombia. I thought a presumption of future persecution arises only after past persecution is shown, and then the government can rebut it through safe relocation. If there is no past persecution finding, who has the burden to show relocation is or is not reasonable? Also, why is the fact that they stayed three weeks at Jimenez's mother's home considered meaningful evidence of safe relocation, rather than just a temporary hiding place?

questions.title: Why does losing on the asylum claim automatically mean losing withholding of removal here?
questions.question_body: At the end, the court says that because Petitioners failed to demonstrate a well-founded fear of persecution for asylum, they necessarily failed to meet the higher standard for withholding of removal. I thought asylum and withholding are distinct forms of relief, with withholding being mandatory if the standard is met. Is the court saying this only because the same factual failures (no persecution, no nexus, no government inability/unwillingness, relocation possible) defeat both claims? Or are there situations where an applicant can lose asylum but still win withholding?

questions.title: Is the court's refusal to address the particular social group and CAT arguments a waiver issue, an exhaustion issue, or both?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Petitioners argued nexus based on both political opinion and particular social group, but then the court says they did not brief the existence of a particular social group or their membership in it, so review was limited to political opinion. It also notes they did not appeal the CAT denial or the due process claim. I'm trying to separate the doctrines here: when does an issue get rejected because it was not exhausted before the BIA, and when is it considered waived because it was not adequately briefed in the court of appeals?
